paras: The threatened lynching of Bud Scipio was a pursuit in July 1903 by a posse of citizens of Coffeyville, Kansas, who said they would lynch Scipio, a Black man accused of assaulting Mrs. Maud Walker, a white woman, on July 15. Scipio escaped into Indian Territory and was captured a week later at Nowata, then returned to Coffeyville, where no mob demonstration was reported and he was committed to jail to await a preliminary hearing. Kansas papers carried the pursuit under headlines such as "Are Bent on Lynching," and the wire version ran as far as Missouri and West Virginia.
Scipio, whose surname the papers also spelled "Scypo" and "Scipro," was described by the Topeka State Journal as "a well known Coffeyville negro" who was married to a white woman.

According to a Coffeyville dispatch to the Topeka State Journal, on Wednesday, July 15, while her husband was absent, Scipio called Mrs. Walker out of the tent where she lived just south of town, put her into a buggy and drove to a field about a mile away, where "it is alleged" he assaulted her. The Wichita Daily Eagle's dispatch said she had been called to her door and "forcibly taken" to the field, and that her injuries were severe. He drove her back to the tent and escaped, and after she gave the alarm a posse started after him.

By the Wichita account, Scipio fled into Indian Territory, and "a large posse of citizens" in pursuit said they would lynch him when he was caught. The Topeka paper wrote that Coffeyville was "thoroughly aroused" and that he would "undoubtedly be lynched" if captured. A State Ledger brief reported that Scipio, with his wife and child, had taken a train to Bartlesville, Indian Territory, where Deputy Sheriff Harbout went to organize a posse to capture him.

Scipio was finally taken at Nowata, Indian Territory, by a man named Carter, called "City Marshal Carter, of Nowata" in the Topeka account and "George Carter and his son" in the Wichita one. His white wife was with him, and he made no resistance.

Back in Coffeyville, Scipio was taken before Judge Perkins and committed to the county jail until a preliminary trial set for the following Monday. The Wichita Daily Eagle said a small crowd greeted him with "black looks" as Deputy Habourt led him, handcuffed, to the train. The Topeka State Journal wrote that Scipio "feared mob violence," but that no demonstration was made, "the cooler heads advising to let the law take its course." No report of the preliminary hearing, a trial or a verdict appears in the coverage.

The first wire version appeared in the Wichita Daily Eagle on July 16 under the headline "Scipio Escapes. Posse Is After the Negro Bent on Lynching," and the same day in the Wheeling Register in West Virginia. The Laclede Blade in Missouri ran it on July 18 as "After Another Negro," with a subhead calling the accused "a Scoundrel." The Topeka State Journal's fuller version, headed "Are Bent on Lynching," hedged the charge with "it is alleged" and described Scipio as "a powerful, coal black negro"; the Dodge City Globe-Republican reprinted it as a "Special" on July 30.

The capture reports dropped that hedge and called him "the negro who criminally assaulted" Mrs. Walker. The Wichita paper also wrote that his wife was viewed "with a mixture of scorn and disgust" and was "anything but good looking," and that the couple had been "begging and stealing for a living" since leaving the city. The only Black-press item found, in the State Ledger of September 26, 1903, was a short Coffeyville item about the search, printed without comment, that called Scipio "the negro who assaulted Maude Walker."

The contemporary dispatches and the Wichita capture report place the alleged assault on Wednesday, but the Dodge City reprint gives "about 3 o'clock Thursday morning." The Topeka paper said Scipio was brought back on Tuesday; the Wichita dispatch of July 22 said he was captured "last night" and returned "this morning." The State Ledger item, dated two months after the capture, still describes Scipio as at large, without explaining the delay.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Bud Scipio
bases: A posse of citizens pursued a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman and said it would lynch him when caught (A1, A2); he was captured by officers a week later and jailed with no mob action reported (A5, A6), so this is a threatened lynching only.

A 'large posse of citizens' said it would lynch Scipio over an assault accusation, an extralegal threat by a group under a pretext of justice (A1, A2), but no one was killed: he was captured, jailed and held for a preliminary hearing with no demonstration (A5, A6).

Two separately written dispatches (A1, A2) agree on the accusation, the escape and the posse's lynching intent, and two separately written capture reports (A5, A6) agree on the capture at Nowata and the absence of mob action.

framing.detail: The first wire version ran as 'Scipio Escapes. Posse Is After the Negro Bent on Lynching' (Wichita), in the Wheeling Register, and as 'After Another Negro ... Assaulted by a Scoundrel' (Laclede, Mo.).

The Topeka State Journal headed its dispatch 'Are Bent on Lynching', hedged the charge with 'it is alleged', and described Scipio as 'a powerful, coal black negro' married to a white woman; its capture report credited 'cooler heads'.
The Wichita capture report stated the assault as fact, reported 'black looks' from the crowd without endorsing violence, and treated his white wife with 'scorn and disgust'.
The State Ledger ran a short Coffeyville news item without headline comment or editorial, repeating 'the negro who assaulted Maude Walker'.
